title: Headquarters of Saudi Aramco hit as Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis trade fresh strikes | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis traded fresh strikes on energy infrastructure, with the Iran-backed group again targeting the Saudi capital and appearing to hit the headquarters of Saudistate oil giant Aramco.

Saudi authorities said an administrative building belonging to Aramco in the Eastern Province city of Dhahran, where the company is headquartered, was targeted. It caused a limited fire, but it’s unclear whether this was due to a direct hit or falling debris. No injuries were reported.

The Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles and two drones targeting the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. At least four people were injured from falling debris, according to Saudi authorities.

Striking Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest crude oil producer, threatens the backbone of the kingdom’s economy and a critical source of global energy supplies. Even without disrupting output, an attack raises fears that escalation could hit Saudi revenues and drive up oil prices worldwide.

CNN has reached out to Saudi Aramco for comment.

The attack marked the latest escalation between the two sides, following a week of deadly Houthi missile and drone attacks that shut Riyadh’smain international airport.

The strikes also came just hours after Saudi Arabia attacked a key fuel depot in Yemen on Tuesday, which it claims was being used by Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities – as well as attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.

Earlier, the Houthi-controlled Yemen Oil Company said the facility held no petroleum products and that an attack would not affect fuel reserves or supplies.

The strikes killed two civilians and injured two, according to the Houthis, though the Saudi-led coalition insisted it had warned civilians to leave the area beforehand.

“This operation focused on neutralizing the capabilities the Houthi militia uses to threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime corridors,” coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.

On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said that Saudi defenses intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh.

Later in the day, the Houthis warned that they will continue to target Saudi airports and oil facilities in the coming days.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree renewed a warning to global shipping companies as well as civilians working there and in Saudi Arabia’s airports to evacuate the facilities immediately.

Tuesday’s exchange comes amid signs that the long-running conflict, which reignited this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm, continues to escalate.

Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward its eastern province, and another aimed at Haradh near the Yemeni border. It also reported intercepting three Houthi drones north of Riyadh.

Meanwhile, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that artillery fire by the Saudi-led coalition in Saada province wounded three Yemenis and two African residents in Baqim district. It later reported that two civilians were killed and two others wounded by artillery fire on residential villages in the border district of Shada in Sadaa, and also reported strikes in Sanaa and several other provinces. CNN cannot independently verify the reports.

The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that — in response to what they say is retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital — they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom.

Those attacks have stepped up in recent days, including withrepeated strikeson Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded on Saturday in what was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries now warning their citizens against using the airport. Meanwhile, the US State Department on Tuesday expanded travel restrictions for US government personnel in the kingdom, saying employees now require special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.

The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’sdefense capabilitiesas it wages its air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.

On Tuesday, the Yemeni government forces claimed to have made continued advances in the military operation, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen.” It said that in the past 24 hours its forces had carried out 2,200 strikes against Houthi positions, killing about 1,200 fighters and destroying or disabling more than 440 military vehicles and other assets. CNN could not independently verify the figures.

Meanwhile, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz continued to rise. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Wednesday it received two late reports that container ships were struck on Tuesday by unidentified projectiles while transiting the chokepoint.

CNN’s Eyad Kourdi and Sarah Tamimi contributed to this report.

CNN’s Eyad Kourdi and Sarah Tamimi contributed to this report.
